method: Selected research records, abstracts, accessible source sections and public guidance checked on 2 and 8 November 2026. Access scope and date are recorded per source; this is not a systematic review. Source wording, questionnaires, diagnostic checklists, figures and recordings are not reproduced. Explanations and fictional examples are original editorial writing.

gilbert.title: Gilbert & Malone (1995). The correspondence bias.
gilbert.explanation: Psychologists Daniel Gilbert and Patrick Malone reviewed research on correspondence bias: people can underweight circumstances when explaining another person’s behaviour.
gilbert.limit: This does not establish that a particular judgment about someone’s character is mistaken.
gilbert.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

kunda.title: Kunda (1990). The case for motivated reasoning.
kunda.explanation: Psychologist Ziva Kunda reviewed research on motivated reasoning. Desired conclusions can shape which reasons people search for and find convincing.
kunda.limit: Disagreement alone cannot establish a hidden motive, and a desired conclusion can still be correct.
kunda.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

eyal.title: Eyal, Steffel & Epley (2018). Perspective mistaking: Accurately understanding the mind of another requires getting perspective, not taking perspective.
eyal.explanation: Tal Eyal and colleagues tested interpersonal predictions across a series of experiments. Imagining another person’s perspective did not consistently improve accuracy; a final experiment found that obtaining information through conversation helped.
eyal.limit: Conversation does not guarantee honesty, complete understanding or safety. These were specific prediction tasks, not tests of every relationship.
eyal.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

listening.title: Itzchakov, Kluger & Castro (2017). I Am Aware of My Inconsistencies but Can Tolerate Them: The Effect of High Quality Listening on Speakers' Attitude Ambivalence.
listening.explanation: Guy Itzchakov and colleagues manipulated listening quality in four laboratory experiments. Attentive, nonjudgmental listening reduced speakers’ social anxiety and helped them recognise mixed attitudes in the studied tasks.
listening.limit: The experiments do not show that listening guarantees agreement or repairs a harmful relationship.
listening.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

memory.title: Loftus (2005). Planting misinformation in the human mind: a 30-year investigation of the malleability of memory.
memory.explanation: Elizabeth Loftus reviewed experimental research on misinformation after an event. Later suggestions can change what people report remembering.
memory.limit: This does not show that a particular memory is false, or justify dismissing an account of harm.
memory.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

stress.title: Shields, Sazma & Yonelinas (2016). The effects of acute stress on core executive functions: A meta-analysis and comparison with cortisol.
stress.explanation: Grant Shields and colleagues combined studies of acute stress and executive functions. Stress tended to impair working memory and flexible switching; effects on inhibition were more mixed.
stress.limit: Laboratory averages cannot explain a particular person’s sharp response or remove responsibility for harm.
stress.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

flexibility.title: Bonanno & Burton (2013). Regulatory Flexibility: An Individual Differences Perspective on Coping and Emotion Regulation.
flexibility.explanation: George Bonanno and Charles Burton reviewed coping and emotion-regulation research. Their framework emphasises noticing context, having several response options and adjusting to feedback.
flexibility.limit: It is a framework with acknowledged measurement limits, not evidence that one response or this worksheet always works.
flexibility.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

bigfive.title: Soto & John (2017). The next Big Five Inventory (BFI-2): Developing and assessing a hierarchical model with 15 facets to enhance bandwidth, fidelity, and predictive power.
bigfive.explanation: Christopher Soto and Oliver John developed and tested the BFI-2 across three studies, organising personality descriptions into five broad dimensions and narrower facets.
bigfive.limit: These are dimensions, not fixed types or clinical diagnoses. This entry does not reproduce, administer or score the questionnaire.
bigfive.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

states.title: Fleeson (2001). Toward a structure- and process-integrated view of personality: traits as density distribution of states.
states.explanation: William Fleeson used repeated reports of everyday behaviour in three studies. Individuals varied considerably across occasions while showing stable differences in their average patterns.
states.limit: A few memorable events cannot establish a lifelong trait; self-reports and the sampled settings have limits.
states.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

habit.title: Wood & Rünger (2016). Psychology of Habit.
habit.explanation: Wendy Wood and Dennis Rünger reviewed habit research. Repetition in recurring contexts can make responses more automatic, alongside deliberate goals.
habit.limit: Not every repeated action is a habit. A pattern may also reflect ongoing constraints, decisions or coercion.
habit.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

culture.title: Vignoles and colleagues (2016). Beyond the 'east-west' dichotomy: Global variation in cultural models of selfhood.
culture.explanation: Vivian Vignoles and colleagues conducted two multinational surveys. Ways of being independent and connected varied across several dimensions, beyond a simple East–West division.
culture.limit: Group patterns cannot reveal one person’s values, and national averages are not instructions for interacting with an individual.
culture.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

weird.title: Henrich, Heine & Norenzayan (2010). The weirdest people in the world?
weird.explanation: Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan compared behavioural findings across populations and examined reliance on Western, educated samples.
weird.limit: Findings from a narrow sample need checking before they are generalised; the review does not assign a personality to a culture.
weird.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

deception.title: Bond & DePaulo (2006). Accuracy of deception judgments.
deception.explanation: Charles Bond and Bella DePaulo combined studies of unaided truth–lie judgments. Average accuracy was about 54%, with truths recognised more accurately than lies.
deception.limit: This is an average across tasks, not the probability that a particular person is lying.
deception.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

nonverbal.title: Vrij, Hartwig & Granhag (2019). Reading Lies: Nonverbal Communication and Deception.
nonverbal.explanation: Aldert Vrij, Maria Hartwig and Pär Granhag reviewed nonverbal deception research. Available behavioural cues were faint and unreliable for practical lie detection.
nonverbal.limit: Nervousness, eye contact or confidence cannot settle whether an account is accurate.
nonverbal.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

intentions.title: Webb & Sheeran (2006). Does changing behavioral intentions engender behavior change? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence.
intentions.explanation: Thomas Webb and Paschal Sheeran combined 47 experimental tests in which intentions changed. Changes in behaviour were generally smaller than changes in intention.
intentions.limit: The result supports separating a promise from follow-through, not deciding why an individual failed to act.
intentions.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

planning.title: Hagger & Luszczynska (2014). Implementation intention and action planning interventions in health contexts: state of the research and proposals for the way forward.
planning.explanation: Martin Hagger and Aleksandra Luszczynska reviewed action-planning interventions in health settings, including differences in results and study quality.
planning.limit: A concrete plan may be useful, but health-intervention findings do not validate a family or workplace agreement.
planning.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

progress.title: Harkin and colleagues (2016). Does monitoring goal progress promote goal attainment? A meta-analysis of the experimental evidence.
progress.explanation: Benjamin Harkin and colleagues combined 138 experiments. Interventions that increased monitoring of goal progress improved goal attainment on average.
progress.limit: Monitoring a chosen goal is different from surveillance of another person; the review did not test this book’s complete method.
progress.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

incentives.title: Cerasoli, Nicklin & Ford (2014). Intrinsic motivation and extrinsic incentives jointly predict performance: a 40-year meta-analysis.
incentives.explanation: Christopher Cerasoli and colleagues combined research on motivation, incentives and performance. Intrinsic motivation and incentives both mattered, with differences between quality and quantity.
incentives.limit: Rewards are neither universally helpful nor universally harmful; performance findings cannot identify one person’s values.
incentives.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

student-motivation.title: Howard and colleagues (2021). Student Motivation and Associated Outcomes: A Meta-Analysis From Self-Determination Theory.
student-motivation.explanation: Joshua Howard and colleagues combined studies of student motivation and outcomes. Different forms of motivation showed different associations with learning and well-being.
student-motivation.limit: Many associations are not causal; applying the findings outside education requires care.
student-motivation.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

sdt.title: Ryan & Deci (2000). Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being.
sdt.explanation: Richard Ryan and Edward Deci reviewed self-determination theory and evidence concerning autonomy, competence and relatedness in motivation and well-being.
sdt.limit: The framework suggests distinctions to investigate. It cannot identify the cause of a particular action or refusal.
sdt.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

belonging.title: Baumeister & Leary (1995). The need to belong: desire for interpersonal attachments as a fundamental human motivation.
belonging.explanation: Roy Baumeister and Mark Leary reviewed evidence for a widespread motivation to form and maintain stable interpersonal attachments.
belonging.limit: The review does not imply that everyone wants the same amount or form of contact, or must maintain an unsafe relationship.
belonging.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

comb.title: Michie, van Stralen & West (2011). The behaviour change wheel: a new method for characterising and designing behaviour change interventions.
comb.explanation: Susan Michie and colleagues reviewed behaviour-change frameworks and proposed COM-B: capability, opportunity and motivation as interacting conditions for behaviour. They examined its use in tobacco-control and obesity policy.
comb.limit: It is a framework for analysing and designing change, not a diagnostic test or proof that one identified barrier caused an action.
comb.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

heritability.title: Polderman and colleagues (2015). Meta-analysis of the heritability of human traits based on fifty years of twin studies.
heritability.explanation: Tinca Polderman and colleagues combined twin-study findings across many human traits. Genetic contributions to variation were widespread across the studied traits.
heritability.limit: Heritability concerns variation in studied populations, not the genetic percentage of one action. Family resemblance does not separate inheritance from learning.
heritability.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

selfchange.title: Roberts and colleagues (2017). A systematic review of personality trait change through intervention.
selfchange.explanation: Brent Roberts and colleagues reviewed 207 intervention studies tracking personality measures, mainly in clinical settings. Trait scores could change, especially emotional stability, and some changes persisted at follow-up.
selfchange.limit: Study designs varied. This does not show that wishing, a short exercise or changing a relative will produce the same result.
selfchange.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

reactance.title: Steindl and colleagues (2015). Understanding Psychological Reactance: New Developments and Findings.
reactance.explanation: Christina Steindl and colleagues reviewed psychological-reactance research on responses to perceived threats to freedom.
reactance.limit: Reactance is one possible process, not an explanation established whenever someone resists a request. Real disagreement and unsuitable demands still matter.
reactance.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

shame.title: Tangney, Stuewig & Mashek (2007). Moral emotions and moral behavior.
shame.explanation: June Tangney and colleagues reviewed theory and research on moral emotions, including distinctions between evaluating one’s whole self and evaluating a particular action.
shame.limit: Emotions have different effects across contexts. An observer cannot read shame, guilt or remorse directly from a facial expression.
shame.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

perfectionism.title: Limburg and colleagues (2017). The Relationship Between Perfectionism and Psychopathology: A Meta-Analysis.
perfectionism.explanation: Karina Limburg and colleagues combined 284 studies of perfectionism and mental-health outcomes. Perfectionistic concerns and strivings were associated with several difficulties.
perfectionism.limit: Associations do not diagnose a disorder or mean that careful work and high standards are inherently harmful.
perfectionism.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

rejection-foundation.title: Downey & Feldman (1996). Implications of rejection sensitivity for intimate relationships.
rejection-foundation.explanation: Geraldine Downey and Scott Feldman used several studies to examine anxious expectations of rejection, interpretations of ambiguous behaviour and intimate-relationship outcomes.
rejection-foundation.limit: The findings do not establish that a particular fear is mistaken or allow this entry to score someone’s rejection sensitivity.
rejection-foundation.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

fairness.title: Colquitt and colleagues (2001). Justice at the millennium: a meta-analytic review of 25 years of organizational justice research.
fairness.explanation: Jason Colquitt and colleagues combined 183 organisational-justice studies. Fair outcomes, procedures, interpersonal treatment and information were related but distinguishable aspects of perceived fairness.
fairness.limit: Most evidence concerns organisations. Disagreement about fairness is not proof of dishonesty or a single objectively correct allocation.
fairness.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

status.title: Anderson, Hildreth & Howland (2015). Is the desire for status a fundamental human motive? A review of the empirical literature.
status.explanation: Cameron Anderson and colleagues reviewed evidence on the desire for respect, admiration and voluntary deference, distinguishing status from power, money and belonging.
status.limit: A broad motive does not explain every interruption, disagreement or wish for recognition.
status.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

autistic-communication.title: Crompton and colleagues (2020). Autistic peer-to-peer information transfer is highly effective.
autistic-communication.explanation: Catherine Crompton and colleagues studied story-information transfer in autistic, non-autistic and mixed groups. Transfer and rapport were poorer in mixed groups than within same-neurotype groups in this task.
autistic-communication.limit: This supports attention to communication fit, not a rule about every autistic person or all forms of neurodivergence.
autistic-communication.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

uncertainty-review.title: Shihata and colleagues (2016). Intolerance of uncertainty in emotional disorders: What uncertainties remain?
uncertainty-review.explanation: Sarah Shihata and colleagues reviewed what was known and unresolved about intolerance of uncertainty across emotional disorders.
uncertainty-review.limit: Uncertainty can be difficult without implying a disorder. The review does not establish what level of uncertainty another person should tolerate.
uncertainty-review.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

avoidance-review.title: Hofmann & Hay (2018). Rethinking avoidance: Toward a balanced approach to avoidance in treating anxiety disorders.
avoidance-review.explanation: Stefan Hofmann and Angela Hay reviewed avoidance in anxiety treatment, including circumstances in which avoidance can be adaptive.
avoidance-review.limit: Function and actual danger matter. This is not a reason to remove someone’s safety arrangements or conduct exposure treatment yourself.
avoidance-review.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

gaslighting.title: Sweet (2019). The Sociology of Gaslighting.
gaslighting.explanation: Sociologist Paige Sweet used domestic-violence accounts to develop an explanation of gaslighting involving power and structural inequalities.
gaslighting.limit: This is a qualitative sociological analysis, not a validated checklist for classifying any disagreement.
gaslighting.access: Publisher-supplied abstract and bibliographic record read through Crossref.

apology.title: Lewicki, Polin & Lount (2016). An Exploration of the Structure of Effective Apologies.
apology.explanation: Roy Lewicki and colleagues ran two studies of how people judged apologies after hypothetical trust violations. Apologies differed in perceived effectiveness depending on what they contained and the kind of violation.
apology.limit: Judging a scenario differs from rebuilding trust after real harm. No apology formula obliges forgiveness or renewed access.
apology.access: Publisher-supplied abstract and bibliographic record read through Crossref.

exchange.title: Cropanzano & Mitchell (2005). Social Exchange Theory: An Interdisciplinary Review.
exchange.explanation: Russell Cropanzano and Marie Mitchell reviewed social-exchange theory in organisational research, including different exchange rules, resources and relationships.
exchange.limit: The review also identifies conceptual ambiguity. Relationships cannot be reduced to a universal ledger of favours.
exchange.access: Publisher-supplied abstract and bibliographic record read through Crossref.

anthropology.title: Lareau (2002). Invisible Inequality: Social Class and Childrearing in Black Families and White Families.
anthropology.explanation: Sociologist Annette Lareau used ethnographic observation and interviews with US families to examine how class-related practices affected interactions with institutions.
anthropology.limit: The study concerns particular families and settings; it is not a universal parenting typology or an explanation of an individual family.
anthropology.access: Publisher-supplied abstract and bibliographic record read through Crossref.

nhs-abuse.title: NHS: Domestic violence and abuse
nhs-abuse.explanation: NHS public guidance describes emotional, physical, sexual and economic abuse and routes to confidential support.
nhs-abuse.limit: Services are UK-specific. It is guidance, not a test that determines a person’s motive or an individual safety assessment.
nhs-abuse.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

coercion-guidance.title: Home Office: Controlling or coercive behaviour — statutory guidance
coercion-guidance.explanation: Home Office statutory guidance describes controlling or coercive behaviour as an unfolding pattern and discusses restrictions, threats, economic abuse and effects on everyday freedom.
coercion-guidance.limit: It addresses law and practice in England and Wales. This book does not establish whether a legal offence occurred or replace local advice.
coercion-guidance.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

nhs-pd.title: NHS: Personality disorder
nhs-pd.explanation: NHS clinical information describes enduring difficulties in relating, thinking, feeling or behaving that cause distress or problems in daily life, with support and treatment options.
nhs-pd.limit: It is general guidance; diagnosis requires professional assessment of the person, history, context and alternatives.
nhs-pd.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

nimh-ocd.title: NIMH: Obsessive-compulsive disorder
nimh-ocd.explanation: NIMH public information describes recurring intrusive obsessions, compulsions or both, their potential impact on daily life and available treatment approaches.
nimh-ocd.limit: This is clinical guidance, not a questionnaire or a way to diagnose someone from cleanliness, checking or an unwanted thought.
nimh-ocd.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

nimh-bpd.title: NIMH: Borderline personality disorder
nimh-bpd.explanation: NIMH public guidance describes difficulties involving emotions, self-image, impulsivity and relationships; presentations vary and effective treatments are available.
nimh-bpd.limit: Risk factors are not individual causes. A professional assessment considers the wider history and possible co-occurring or alternative conditions.
nimh-bpd.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

nimh-depression.title: NIMH: Depression
nimh-depression.explanation: NIMH public guidance distinguishes passing low feelings from depression that can significantly affect thinking, sleep, eating, work and other daily activities.
nimh-depression.limit: Only assessment can establish the explanation of a particular change; quietness or withdrawal alone is insufficient.
nimh-depression.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

nimh-anxiety.title: NIMH: Anxiety disorders
nimh-anxiety.explanation: NIMH public guidance distinguishes occasional anxiety from difficulties that persist, spread or interfere with ordinary activities.
nimh-anxiety.limit: It does not make repeated reassurance or avoidance a diagnosis. Support depends on the person’s actual difficulties.
nimh-anxiety.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

nimh-trauma.title: NIMH: Post-traumatic stress disorder
nimh-trauma.explanation: NIMH public guidance explains that reactions after trauma vary and that persistent symptoms affecting life can warrant assessment and treatment.
nimh-trauma.limit: Not everyone exposed to trauma develops PTSD, and observers cannot infer a trauma history from an action.
nimh-trauma.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

nimh-support.title: NIMH: Caring for your mental health
nimh-support.explanation: NIMH public guidance recommends considering distress, persistence and interference with usual activities when seeking help.
nimh-support.limit: US service information may not apply elsewhere; support should be adapted to local options and urgency.
nimh-support.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

nimh-adolescence.title: NIMH: The teen brain — 7 things to know
nimh-adolescence.explanation: NIMH public guidance describes adolescence as a period of continuing development, learning, changing social experience and sleep needs.
nimh-adolescence.limit: Broad developmental patterns do not establish an individual teenager’s judgment, motives or capacity.
nimh-adolescence.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

nhs-grief.title: NHS: Grief after bereavement or loss
nhs-grief.explanation: NHS public guidance describes varied responses to loss and ways to seek support when grief is difficult to manage.
nhs-grief.limit: There is no compulsory sequence of feelings or timetable that every grieving person must follow.
nhs-grief.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

cdc-development.title: CDC: Developmental milestones
cdc-development.explanation: CDC public guidance describes development in play, learning, communication, action and movement, and recommends discussing concerns or lost skills with a clinician.
cdc-development.limit: Its milestone resources are not substitutes for validated screening and do not diagnose a child from one missed task.
cdc-development.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

nhs-confusion.title: NHS: Sudden confusion
nhs-confusion.explanation: NHS guidance treats sudden new confusion as requiring urgent medical assessment because several medical causes are possible.
nhs-confusion.limit: It is UK guidance; use the appropriate urgent medical service where you are rather than trying to infer a psychological motive.
nhs-confusion.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

eeoc-harassment.title: US EEOC: Harassment
eeoc-harassment.explanation: The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission describes harassment linked to protected characteristics and retaliation within the laws it administers.
eeoc-harassment.limit: Legal definitions, coverage and procedures vary by jurisdiction. Unfair or harmful conduct can still matter when it does not meet this legal definition.
eeoc-harassment.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

msd-pd-narcissistic.title: MSD Manual: Narcissistic personality disorder
msd-pd-narcissistic.explanation: The MSD Manual’s public clinical overview explains this condition in the context of an enduring pattern, effects on functioning and professional assessment.
msd-pd-narcissistic.limit: This is explanatory clinical guidance, not a checklist to apply to relatives. The short examples and response suggestions here are editorial, not diagnostic criteria.
msd-pd-narcissistic.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

msd-pd-histrionic.explanation: The MSD Manual’s public clinical overview explains this condition in the context of an enduring pattern, effects on functioning and professional assessment.

msd-pd-schizoid.explanation: The MSD Manual’s public clinical overview explains this condition in the context of an enduring pattern, effects on functioning and professional assessment.

msd-pd-schizotypal.explanation: The MSD Manual’s public clinical overview explains this condition in the context of an enduring pattern, effects on functioning and professional assessment.

msd-pd-ocpd.explanation: The MSD Manual’s public clinical overview explains this condition in the context of an enduring pattern, effects on functioning and professional assessment.
msd-pd-ocpd.limit: This is explanatory clinical guidance, not a checklist to apply to relatives. The short examples and response suggestions here are editorial, not diagnostic criteria.
msd-pd-ocpd.access: Relevant sections of the public guidance page read; not an individual assessment or a systematic evidence review.

time-horizons.title: Carstensen LL, Isaacowitz DM, Charles ST. (1999). Taking time seriously. A theory of socioemotional selectivity.
time-horizons.explanation: Laura Carstensen and colleagues developed socioemotional selectivity theory, reviewing how perceived time horizons can shape social goals in younger and older people.
time-horizons.limit: It is a theory with reviewed evidence, not a rule that age determines what an individual wants.
time-horizons.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

ageism.title: Hu RX, Luo M, Zhang A, Li LW. (2021). Associations of Ageism and Health: A Systematic Review of Quantitative Observational Studies.
ageism.explanation: Hu and colleagues reviewed quantitative observational studies of ageism and health. Age-related stereotypes, discrimination and self-perceptions were associated with several health outcomes.
ageism.limit: The studies were observational and measures varied; the review does not establish the cause of a particular person’s difficulty.
ageism.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

power.title: Keltner D, Gruenfeld DH, Anderson C. (2003). Power, approach, and inhibition.
power.explanation: Dacher Keltner, Deborah Gruenfeld and Cameron Anderson reviewed theory and evidence connecting unequal power with opportunities, threats and behavioural tendencies.
power.limit: This is a broad framework, not a universal rule about every powerful or less powerful person.
power.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

narcissism-meta.title: Kjærvik SL, Bushman BJ. (2021). The link between narcissism and aggression: A meta-analytic review.
narcissism-meta.explanation: Sophie Kjærvik and Brad Bushman combined 437 studies on narcissism and aggression. Research measures of narcissism were associated with aggression on average, with stronger links in provocation conditions.
narcissism-meta.limit: These average associations do not diagnose a person, establish the cause of one action or predict individual violence. Do not provoke someone to test a trait.
narcissism-meta.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

narcissism-components.title: Du TV, Miller JD, Lynam DR. (2022). The relation between narcissism and aggression: A meta-analysis.
narcissism-components.explanation: Du, Miller and Lynam conducted a preregistered meta-analysis of narcissism components and aggression. Associations differed across components, showing why a single broad label can conceal meaningful differences.
narcissism-components.limit: Research components and measures are not a home classification system. Results cannot identify a clinical disorder or a hidden strategy from an incident log.
narcissism-components.access: Research record and abstract read through Europe PMC; no claim of full-text review.

address.title: Brown & Gilman (1960). The Pronouns of Power and Solidarity.
address.explanation: Roger Brown and Albert Gilman examined how address pronouns express power and solidarity, drawing on historical material and language informants.
address.limit: The mainly European-language material does not show that a particular family uses names deliberately to establish rank.
address.access: Accessible institutional text: introduction and power/solidarity discussion read.

kinship.title: Ember, Droe & Russell (2022). Residence and Kinship.
kinship.explanation: Carol Ember and colleagues summarise cross-cultural research on kinship terms, descent, residence and family organisation. These are related but distinct arrangements.
kinship.limit: Ethnographic group patterns do not determine one household’s practices or justify assuming values from ethnicity.
kinship.access: HRAF overview and sections on residence, descent and kin terminology read.

presupposition.title: Potts (2014 draft). Presupposition and Implicature.
presupposition.explanation: Linguist Christopher Potts explains how language can carry background assumptions and implied meanings alongside its main assertion. Context affects how these are understood.
presupposition.limit: This is a linguistics handbook draft, not a test of manipulative intent. Indirect or presupposing language is also routine communication.
presupposition.access: Introduction and presupposition sections of the author’s accessible draft read.

authority.title: Stevanovic & Peräkylä (2012). Deontic Authority in Interaction.
authority.explanation: Melisa Stevanovic and Anssi Peräkylä analysed recorded workplace planning discussions. People could accept a plan while resisting another speaker’s assumed right to decide it.
authority.limit: Conversation analysis of a specific workplace does not establish every family’s decision rights or validate a tactic detector.
authority.access: Institutional research record and abstract read.

facework.title: Cardon & Okoro (2010). A Meta-Analysis of the Cultural Propositions about Conflict Management Styles in Face-Negotiation Theory.
facework.explanation: Peter Cardon and Ephraim Okoro reviewed studies testing cultural propositions about conflict styles and face: the respect or social identity people seek to maintain in interaction.
facework.limit: The accessible abstract describes the review’s questions without detailed results. No country-specific prediction or claim that a face-saving technique works is drawn from it.
facework.access: Institutional abstract and bibliographic record only; detailed results not reviewed.

family-boundary.title: Carroll, Olson & Buckmiller (2007). Family Boundary Ambiguity: A 30-Year Review.
family-boundary.explanation: Jason Carroll and colleagues reviewed 37 studies across settings including divorce, stepfamilies, illness and caregiving. Boundary ambiguity concerns uncertainty about family membership or roles.
family-boundary.limit: This differs from deciding a personal limit. The review does not supply a checklist for assigning family roles or blame.
family-boundary.access: Institutional abstract and research record read.

differential.title: Jensen & Thomsen (2024). Parental differential treatment of siblings linked with internalizing and externalizing behavior: A meta-analysis.
differential.explanation: Jensen and Thomsen combined research involving 26,451 participants. Differences in parental treatment were associated with children’s internalising and externalising difficulties.
differential.limit: The largely White child/adolescent samples do not establish an adult in-law’s motive, and association does not identify a single cause.
differential.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

mental-work.title: Daminger (2019). The Cognitive Dimension of Household Labor.
mental-work.explanation: Sociologist Allison Daminger used interviews with members of 35 couples to examine cognitive household work, including anticipating needs, identifying options and monitoring progress.
mental-work.limit: This qualitative study offers distinctions for examining work. It is not a population estimate or a rule about what women or men always do.
mental-work.access: Publisher abstract read; full interview methods and article not reviewed.

demand-withdraw.title: Schrodt, Witt & Shimkowski (2014). A Meta-Analytical Review of the Demand/Withdraw Pattern of Interaction.
demand-withdraw.explanation: Paul Schrodt and colleagues combined 74 studies linking demand–withdraw interaction with relational, communication and individual outcomes. The sequence concerns one person pressing for change while another disengages.
demand-withdraw.limit: The associations do not establish who caused a conflict or equal responsibility for harm.
demand-withdraw.access: Abstract read through EBSCO bibliographic record; publisher full text restricted.

cycle-context.title: Ross and colleagues (2019). Communication that is maladaptive for middle-class couples is adaptive for socioeconomically disadvantaged couples.
cycle-context.explanation: Jaclyn Ross and colleagues followed couples over time. Associations between demand–withdraw communication and relationship satisfaction varied with socioeconomic resources.
cycle-context.limit: These observational studies do not prescribe withdrawal or excuse coercion; practical capacity can change what a request and response mean.
cycle-context.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

responsiveness.title: Arican-Dinc & Gable (2023). Responsiveness in romantic partners’ interactions.
responsiveness.explanation: Arican-Dinc and Gable reviewed perceived responsiveness: feeling that a partner understands, validates and cares about what one has shared.
responsiveness.limit: Romantic-interaction research does not validate a universal support script. Validation of an experience need not mean agreement with every factual claim.
responsiveness.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

family-response.title: Cook, Dezangré & De Mol (2018). Sources of perceived responsiveness in family relationships.
family-response.explanation: William Cook and colleagues studied 207 two-parent, two-child families. Perceived responsiveness reflected contributions from the perceiver, the other person and their particular relationship.
family-response.limit: The design does not establish a causal remedy or represent all family structures. One interaction is not simply a personality reading.
family-response.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

needs-support.title: Slemp and colleagues (2024). Interpersonal supports for basic psychological needs and their relations with motivation, well-being, and performance.
needs-support.explanation: Gavin Slemp and colleagues combined 881 independent samples. Support for autonomy, competence and relatedness was associated with need satisfaction, well-being and performance.
needs-support.limit: These associations support considering several kinds of support together; they do not validate this book’s exercises or establish the cause of one refusal.
needs-support.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

leader-support.title: Slemp and colleagues (2018). Leader autonomy support in the workplace: A meta-analytic review.
leader-support.explanation: Gavin Slemp and colleagues combined 83 unique workplace samples. Perceived autonomy-supportive supervision was associated with autonomous motivation, well-being and positive work behaviour.
leader-support.limit: The largely correlational evidence cannot determine whether one manager’s oversight is excessive or show that removing all checks improves work.
leader-support.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

sequential.title: Burger (1999). The foot-in-the-door compliance procedure: a multiple-process analysis and review.
sequential.explanation: Jerry Burger reviewed research on small requests followed by larger requests. Several processes may contribute, including consistency, commitment and reactance; conditions can also eliminate or reverse the effect.
sequential.limit: This is not a guaranteed way to obtain agreement or a way to infer a requester’s intent.
sequential.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

request-comparison.title: Pascual & Guéguen (2005). Foot-in-the-door and door-in-the-face: a comparative meta-analytic study.
request-comparison.explanation: Alexandre Pascual and Nicolas Guéguen compared studies of small-then-large and large-then-smaller requests. They found no significant difference between the procedures in those direct comparisons.
request-comparison.limit: Comparing the two procedures does not alone establish that either beats an ordinary request in every setting.
request-comparison.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

norm-messages.title: Papakonstantinou and colleagues (2025). A systematic review and meta-analysis of social norms messaging approaches for improving health behaviours.
norm-messages.explanation: Papakonstantinou and colleagues reviewed 89 trials of social-norm health messages. The apparent average benefit disappeared after adjustment for publication bias.
norm-messages.limit: This finding concerns specific health interventions in developed countries, not whether social norms ever influence people.
norm-messages.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

attachment.title: Zhang and colleagues (2022). The relationship between adult attachment and mental health: A meta-analysis.
attachment.explanation: Zhang and colleagues combined studies of attachment anxiety and avoidance. Both dimensions were associated with mental-health measures.
attachment.limit: The associations do not diagnose anyone or establish a fixed attachment type or childhood cause.
attachment.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

attachment-time.title: Hadden, Smith & Webster (2014). Relationship duration moderates associations between attachment and relationship quality.
attachment-time.explanation: Benjamin Hadden and colleagues reviewed associations between attachment dimensions, relationship satisfaction and commitment. Relationship duration moderated associations in cross-sectional samples.
attachment-time.limit: Differences between longer and shorter relationships do not establish a person’s future or show that duration caused deterioration.
attachment-time.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

daily-plans.title: Sezer and colleagues (2025). An experimental investigation of daily mental contrasting with implementation intentions and goal motives in reducing bedtime procrastination.
daily-plans.explanation: Sezer and colleagues compared daily with one-off planning in a week-long registered study of 297 participants. The daily group reported less bedtime procrastination.
daily-plans.limit: The specific comparison and short duration do not establish a durable treatment for every kind of procrastination.
daily-plans.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

feedback-process.title: Kluger & DeNisi (1996). The effects of feedback interventions on performance.
feedback-process.explanation: Avraham Kluger and Angelo DeNisi combined feedback experiments. Performance improved on average, but more than a third of the interventions reduced it. Their account emphasises where feedback directs attention.
feedback-process.limit: No fixed wording or praise formula follows from the average result; task and context matter.
feedback-process.access: Institutional abstract and research record read.

speak-up.title: Frazier and colleagues (2017). Psychological Safety: A Meta-Analytic Review and Extension.
speak-up.explanation: Lance Frazier and colleagues combined 136 workplace samples to examine psychological safety and its connections with leadership, work behaviour and performance.
speak-up.limit: The evidence does not guarantee that speaking up is safe in a particular organisation or that one invitation will change its consequences.
speak-up.access: Institutional abstract and research record read.

facets.title: Stewart and colleagues (2022). The finer details? The predictability of life outcomes from Big Five domains, facets, and nuances.
facets.explanation: Ross Stewart and colleagues compared broad traits, facets and narrower descriptions when predicting 53 self-reported outcomes in a large dataset with separate training and validation samples. Narrower descriptions carried useful information.
facets.limit: Prediction is not a causal account. The study does not license scoring someone from selected anecdotes or copying assessment items.
facets.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

ostracism.title: Williams (2007). Ostracism.
ostracism.explanation: Kipling Williams reviewed research on being ignored, rejected or excluded. Such experiences can threaten belonging and other needs, with different behavioural responses.
ostracism.limit: A painful exclusion does not establish its cause, and one missed invitation does not prove deliberate ostracism.
ostracism.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

gossip-evidence.title: Grayson, Feinberg, Willer & Zaki (2025). Ironic effects of prosocial gossip in driving inaccurate social perceptions.
gossip-evidence.explanation: Samantha Grayson and colleagues reanalysed economic-game gossip and ran an experiment with new readers. Negative stories were disproportionately shared, leading readers to underestimate how cooperatively the original groups behaved.
gossip-evidence.limit: Economic-game findings do not establish that every warning is biased or that a specific family’s reputation is false.
gossip-evidence.access: Abstract read in Stanford GSB Preserve institutional record: https://gsbpreserve.stanford.edu/view/43150/ironic-effects-of-prosocial-gossip-in-driving-inaccurate-social-perceptions

comparison.title: Social comparison and envy on social media: A critical review (2022).
comparison.explanation: A 2022 critical review examined social comparison, envy and well-being on social media. The evidence included mixed, conditional and person-dependent findings.
comparison.limit: Comparison is not uniformly harmful, and findings about social media cannot explain every offline comparison.
comparison.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

gatekeeping.title: Reis and colleagues (2025). Relations Between Parental Gatekeeping and Parenting in Families With Children: A Scoping Review.
gatekeeping.explanation: Reis and colleagues reviewed 16 studies of parental gatekeeping and parenting. They describe complex, bidirectional relationships and disagreement about concepts and measurement.
gatekeeping.limit: The literature largely concerns coparenting and father involvement. It does not directly establish a grandmother’s or in-law’s strategy.
gatekeeping.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

near-event.title: Shiffman, Stone & Hufford (2008). Ecological momentary assessment.
near-event.explanation: Saul Shiffman and colleagues reviewed repeated sampling of experiences close to the time they occur and in everyday settings. This can reduce reliance on global retrospective reports.
near-event.limit: A private notebook is not a validated assessment or proof of causality. Recording must remain proportionate and should not become surveillance.
near-event.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

individual-inference.title: Fisher, Medaglia & Jeronimus (2018). Lack of group-to-individual generalizability is a threat to human subjects research.
individual-inference.explanation: Aaron Fisher and colleagues examined six repeated-measures datasets and highlighted difficulties transferring aggregate patterns to individual processes.
individual-inference.limit: This is a reason to check individual context and uncertainty, not a claim that population research can never inform individuals; methodological debate continues.
individual-inference.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

ai-agreement.title: Sharma and colleagues. Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (ICLR 2024; arXiv revision 2025).
ai-agreement.explanation: Mrinank Sharma and colleagues evaluated five AI assistants and found that matching a user’s views could compete with giving accurate answers.
ai-agreement.limit: The evaluated models do not represent every current service. A prompt asking for alternatives is not a validated guarantee against sycophancy.
ai-agreement.access: Author abstract and version record read; not a claim of evaluating the app’s current providers.

darvo.title: Harsey & Freyd (2023). The Influence of Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender and Insincere Apologies on Perceptions of Sexual Assault.
darvo.explanation: Sarah Harsey and Jennifer Freyd experimentally varied fictional sexual-assault accounts read by 230 undergraduates. Denial, attack and blame reversal affected judgments of the people described.
darvo.limit: This concerns observers’ judgments in a specific scenario. It is not a test of guilt, family prevalence or personality disorder.
darvo.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

impression.title: Peck & Levashina (2017). Impression Management and Interview and Job Performance Ratings.
impression.explanation: Jennifer Peck and Julia Levashina combined research on impression management in interviews and performance ratings. Associations varied by tactic and research design.
impression.limit: These workplace findings do not establish dishonesty whenever someone changes their presentation across audiences.
impression.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

parentification.title: Dariotis and colleagues (2023). Parentification Vulnerability, Reactivity, Resilience, and Thriving: A Mixed Methods Systematic Literature Review.
parentification.explanation: Jacinda Dariotis and colleagues reviewed 95 studies of young people taking developmentally inappropriate adult-like roles. Outcomes varied with demands, support and other circumstances.
parentification.limit: Family contribution is not automatically parentification. Findings do not determine one adult’s childhood history or imply that every responsibility harms a child.
parentification.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

moral-emotions.title: Tangney, Stuewig & Mashek (2007). Moral emotions and moral behavior.
moral-emotions.explanation: June Tangney and colleagues reviewed shame, guilt and other moral emotions, distinguishing evaluations of the whole self from concern about a specific action.
moral-emotions.limit: These distinctions do not reveal another person’s inner emotion from their behaviour or make anger proof of shame.
moral-emotions.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

digital-tone.title: Kruger, Epley, Parker & Ng (2005). Egocentrism over e-mail: can we communicate as well as we think?
digital-tone.explanation: Justin Kruger and colleagues ran five experiments suggesting that people overestimate how well an intended tone comes across in email.
digital-tone.limit: The experiments do not show that every short message is misunderstood or that a delayed reply is harmless. Contemporary platforms and relationships may differ.
digital-tone.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

negotiation.title: Boothby, Cooney & Schweitzer (2023). Embracing Complexity: A Review of Negotiation Research.
negotiation.explanation: Erica Boothby, Gus Cooney and Maurice Schweitzer reviewed negotiation research, emphasising context, interaction, power and conditions that change familiar effects.
negotiation.limit: The review does not supply a universally effective bargaining script. Mediation requires separate attention to consent, authority and safety.
negotiation.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.

acculturation.title: Shukla and colleagues (2025). When and how do parent-child acculturation gaps matter?
acculturation.explanation: Serena Shukla and colleagues reviewed 98 records concerning immigrant parents and children. More than half found no association between cultural gaps and the examined child, parenting or family outcomes.
acculturation.limit: Different rates of cultural adaptation are not inherently a family problem. Specific domains and circumstances matter.
acculturation.access: NCBI bibliographic record and abstract read; no claim of full-text review.
